statements.quote: Claude AI was introduced to (G1), who trained and got accustomed to its use. (G2) wrote in their own style after being informed about the procedure they would follow. The process begins by copying the provided prompt into the response box. Participants then clicked on the AI's answer. Only participants who wrote using Claude AI then took a screenshot containing the full answer for analyzing them. The prompts given are three stimulating beginnings of stories. The first one is: “Every night, you see a shadowy figure standing at the foot of your bed. No matter what you do, it always appears at the same time, getting closer each night.” The second prompt is: “A little sister receives an old, creepy doll as a gift. Soon after, strange things start happening around the house, and the child insists that the doll is alive.” The third is: “A dense forest near a small town is known for the whispers that can be heard at night. When a local teenager goes missing, a group of friends ventures into the forest to uncover its eerie secrets.”
statements.locator: PDF p. 6, section 3.3 Materials, first paragraph (prompts and Claude screenshots).

statements.quote: The study was conducted during three ordinary sessions of the Bookish Minds club. In each 50-minute session, participants crafted a distinct short horror story. After the allotted time, the written drafts, completed on paper, were collected. Participants (G1) using Claude AI integrated its suggestions into their writing process, while those writing independently (G2) relied solely on their own skills and imagination. This setup allowed for a clear comparison between AI-assisted and human-only creativity in the realm of horror fiction.
statements.locator: PDF pp. 6-7, section 3.3 Materials, second paragraph (paper drafts collected).

statements.quote: The below scales (figure 1) provide a visual representation of the evaluation criteria for key horror elements in the experiment comparing the human mind and Claude AI. Each criterion, fear of the unknown (originality), atmosphere (descriptive language and setting), tension build-up (pacing and suspense), and character depth (relatable characters and fears), is rated on a scale from 1 to 5. A score of 1 indicates a minimal or ineffective application of the element, such as flat characters or a lack of originality, while a score of 5 signifies a highly effective use, such as deeply relatable characters or an immersive atmosphere. Intermediate scores (2.5, 3.75, 4.5) reflect varying degrees of effectiveness, with 2.5 representing basic or minimal qualities and 4.5 denoting strong but not fully exceptional implementation.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7, section 4 Results, first paragraph; Figure 1 on p. 9 (printed evaluation rubric).

statements.quote: The statistics presented in the chart below (figure 2) represent the mean scores of two distinct groups: (G1) utilizing Claude AI, and(G2) composed of human participants, both tasked with crafting short horror stories. The mean scores provide an average evaluation across multiple (3) stories based on specific criteria related to key horror elements. By averaging the scores within each group, the chart offers a clear comparison of how effectively each group performed across these critical aspects of horror writing. This comparison allows for an objective assessment of the relative strengths and weaknesses between human creativity and AI-generated content.
statements.locator: PDF p. 9, section 4 Results, paragraph after Figure 1 (aggregate group scores).

notes:
Read the complete local markdown conversion (262 lines; all 14 PDF pages, including the conclusion and references). There are no appendices, supplementary-file notices, explicit data/code/materials-availability statements, preregistrations, or repository links for this study. No request-for-data offer appears. PDF embedded-file enumeration returned no attachments. Quotes were checked against PyMuPDF text; line wraps and layout whitespace were normalized, including rejoining the printed 50-minute hyphenation.

The statements below describe the study materials, data collection, printed rubric and aggregate results, plus the article license. They do not state that the collected Claude screenshots, handwritten drafts, or individual ratings are publicly shared. The three prompts are printed in section 3.3 (p. 6), the evaluation rubric in section 4 and Figure 1 (pp. 7-9), group summary figures in Figures 2-6 (pp. 10-12), and a few excerpts attributed to student AB from G2 in section 4.1 (pp. 10-11). These in-article materials and excerpts are not counted as a separate deposit or a usable participant-level dataset. The CC BY 4.0 notice applies to the article; no separate data license was found.

The paper DOI https://doi.org/10.21659/rupkatha.v16n3.01 returned HTTP 200 after redirecting to https://rupkatha.com/v16n301/. The publisher landing page loaded without credentials. Its article content and links provide Full-Text PDF and Issue Access, but no supplementary dataset, code, preregistration, or other study-file download. The linked PDF returned HTTP 200. No relevant deposit was identified, so repository file enumeration and data-table inspection were not applicable; no data files were downloaded.

The form's data_and_code.data_url and code_url are both empty, and the provided form has no final object or final.open_items field. The observed missing statistics for S1 therefore cannot be matched to a final.open_items list. No public data were found from which to obtain per-person means across stories, arm-specific SDs or SEs, analyzed participant/output counts, or diversity measures using complete participant-linked texts. The form also records random assignment as not_stated; this availability audit does not establish randomization.

All four requested repository APIs returned successful title and author-name searches after correcting Zenodo's unauthenticated page-size limit. Search entries include the two failed HTTP 400 requests with null result counts and their successful replacements. Repeated identical searches are consolidated. Negative searches cannot exclude an unindexed or private deposit; the specified OSF nodes endpoint searches titles, not contributor names. Confidence is medium for the overall absence finding.

HTTP checks of every distinct HTTP(S) URL in the markdown and PDF link annotations, plus the reference DOI printed without an HTTP prefix and the publisher PDF link, are recorded below. Reference-work URLs are unrelated to this study's data and are not treated as deposits. The markdown omitted the hyphen in the Porto repository host; both the malformed markdown URL and the correct PDF link were checked. The malformed publisher host containing a comma failed DNS; the other publisher link worked. Challenge pages and forbidden responses were not bypassed. The author mailto link was not contacted. No credentials or personal identifiers were sent; requests used User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1.
